summary_paragraph: A man with a history of non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, type I diabetes, COPD, schizophrenia, and chronic crack cocaine use was admitted for acute respiratory distress following progressive dyspnea over 36 hours. He presented with severe shortness of breath, particularly when supine, and was found to have an ejection fraction of 20% on echocardiogram and diffuse bilateral lung opacities on imaging. His respiratory failure was attributed to a combination of acute on chronic systolic heart failure and hypersensitivity pneumonitis likely due to prior crack cocaine use. He was initially managed in the MICU with NIPPV, IV furosemide, and high-dose steroids, then transferred to the general floor. Antibiotics were discontinued after one dose due to lack of infection. His breathing improved rapidly with steroid therapy and diuresis. He was started on a 20-day prednisone taper and required intensified insulin therapy due to steroid-induced hyperglycemia. He was discharged home with his sister, able to ambulate independently on room air, with follow-up arranged for cardiology (AICD evaluation), pulmonary (PFTs and pending hypersensitivity panel), and continuation of his dual diagnosis program for addiction support.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure
Bronchitis and pneumonitis due to fumes and vapors
Diabetes with unspecified complication, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled
